title: Doers of the word (James 1:19–27)
hookLine: swift to hear, slow to speak, and not hearers only

lines: THE HALL MIRROR ON THE WAY OUT.
cards: On your way out the door you catch yourself in the hall mirror. Hair sticking up. Something green in your teeth.
You see it clearly; you even make a face at it. Then your keys are in your hand, the door shuts behind you, and by the time you reach the car the mirror is gone from your mind, and so is the spinach.
Two hours later someone at work tells you. James uses a moment like it, a man and a mirror, to describe the way people listen to God's word.

teach.h: SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.
teach.b: It starts with three speeds. The Douay-Rheims: "let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger." Fast ears, slow mouth, slower temper.
A quarrel runs the other way round. Then the line this passage turns on: "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves."
Hearing can feel like progress. A good homily, a moving reading, a podcast that lands, and it's easy to think, there, that's done. James says that feeling can fool you.

teach.h: THE MAN AT THE MIRROR FORGETS.
teach.b: Here comes the mirror. Someone who hears the word and doesn't do it is like a man who looks at his own face in a glass, walks away, and forgets at once what he looked like.
The word shows you yourself; the question is whether you do anything about what you saw. The Greek for doers is poietai, makers. Greek used the same word for a poet.
So a doer of the word makes something out of what they heard. Then James gets practical. Rein in your tongue.

And he gives a short definition of religion that's hard to wriggle out of: religion that's pure in God's sight is this, "to visit the fatherless and widows in their tribulation," and to keep yourself unstained by the world.

teach.h: BE YE DOERS OF THE WORD.
teach.b: Catholics hear the word at every Mass, and at the end the people are sent out: go. The hearing happens inside. The doing happens on the way home.

how: At every Mass Catholics hear readings from scripture and a homily, and the Mass ends with a dismissal sending the people out; many parishes link the Sunday word to works of mercy such as visiting the sick, the elderly and the bereaved.

doers, makers of what they heard
poets who set Scripture to music

games.q: James on hearing — tap the pairs.

s: James says hearing the word is enough on its own
he says hearers only are deceiving themselves. the word is meant to be done.
James compares the word to a mirror
it shows you yourself. a hearer who doesn't act forgets what he saw.
James defines pure religion partly as visiting orphans and widows
to visit the fatherless and widows in their tribulation, and keep unstained by the world.

games.q: you've just heard a reading that hit home. you feel moved, and part of you feels the job is done. what does James say?
o: good: being moved is the point.
do something with it, or you're fooling yourself.
talk about it with everyone right away.
games.why: James says hearers only deceive themselves. and talking right away isn't it either: he wants people swift to hear and slow to speak.

practice: Let one phrase come back from the last Mass you went to, or any line of scripture from this week; take the first that sticks, not the best.
Ask what it would look like on a Tuesday, a call, a visit, an apology, a meal for someone, and picture yourself doing it: where, when, the first words you'd say.
If you pray, ask for help to do it; if not, just choose it and hold it.

wordCard.voice: Poietai, makers. James one: not hearers only, who see themselves in the mirror and forget, but makers, who do what they heard. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: doers of the word (James 1:22). a poiētēs is a maker; Greek also used the word for a poet.

carryVoice: Your line: doers, not hearers. Makers of something out of what they heard. See you tomorrow.
